title: How Social Media Can Make You Feel Like The Worst Teacher
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin recounts an early-career visit to a colleague's dazzling, elaborately decorated classroom that left him demoralized, only to later learn through team-teaching together that the teacher's polish masked exhaustion, overspending, and a class that was often unfocused despite the impressive projects. He uses this story to critique the curated, highlight-reel version of teaching now amplified by social media, arguing it fosters envy and self-doubt in teachers who compare their ordinary classrooms to others' best moments. He reminds readers that effective teaching rests on three fundamentals—classroom management, high standards, and content knowledge and delivery—none of which require decor or viral projects. He allows that some educators share online in good faith, but urges readers to view most classroom social media as entertainment rather than a benchmark.
points: Tells a personal story of a colleague whose dazzling classroom masked exhaustion and an unfocused, dependent class.
Argues social media amplifies a curated, highlight-reel version of teaching that fosters envy and self-doubt.
Identifies classroom management, high standards, and content knowledge and delivery as the three real pillars of effective teaching.
Notes that much classroom content posted online is driven by views, likes, and comments rather than genuine pedagogical value.
Advises viewing most teaching-related social media as entertainment rather than a benchmark for one's own classroom.
quotes: There was a solar system suspended from the ceiling to perfect scale along with model rockets his students had shot into the sky.

Today, there are scores of “stellar” teachers you can find online to make you feel terrible anytime you like. You can visit them virtually, watch their cheery day-in-the-life, and ogle classrooms that put yours to shame.

Much of what you see today via social media is an illusion. There are deep ulterior motives at work that very rarely reveal the truth: That all that color and beauty and creativity doesn’t necessarily mean you’re an effective teacher.
He was stressed-out and exhausted and spent a boatload of his own money. He easily put in quadruple the amount of time and energy than I did preparing each day.
He said that he put in all that time and effort and made such a big show of his classroom in front of others to make up for what he felt were his inadequacies.
But remind yourself that no one is always so bright and perfect and that all those cute posters and projects are far down on the list of priorities that make for effective teaching.
